explain.say: Imagine you have a big test tomorrow, a football match, and a messy room to tidy. Your body feels like it is buzzing! That is stress: how your body reacts when life asks a lot of you. Look at the body on the board.

explain.say: Short bursts of stress are normal. Long stress needs looking after: move your body, sleep well, talk to someone and break big jobs into small bits. Great work! If stress feels too much, tell a trusted grown-up, a school counsellor or a doctor.

steps.note: A walk, a dance or a game

steps.label: Break it down
steps.note: Do one small piece at a time

faq.a: Stress is how your body and mind react when you face a challenge or pressure, like exams or problems at home. Your body releases chemicals that get you ready for action.

faq.q: Why do my shoulders hurt when I am stressed?
faq.a: Stress tells your muscles to tighten, ready to act. If the stress goes on for a while, those tight muscles in your neck and shoulders can start to ache.
asks: Why do I get headaches when stressed?

faq.a: Moving your body, good sleep, healthy food, talking to someone you trust, and breaking big tasks into small steps all help. So does doing something you enjoy.
asks: How can I deal with stress?

faq.a: No. A little short-term stress can help you focus and do your best, like before a race. It becomes a problem when it is too much or lasts a long time.
Cortisol is a chemical messenger, often called the stress hormone, made by glands on top of your kidneys. It gives you energy in a challenge, but too much for too long can make you tired and unwell.

facts: Cortisol, often called the stress hormone, is made by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys.
The word stress was made popular in medicine by the Hungarian-Canadian scientist Hans Selye in the 1930s.
